title: Four years ago countries made a historic deal to save nature. Is it dead in the water?

As negotiators convene for Cop17, the pressure is on to find a way to honour the commitments made at previous summits Cop17 at a glance: everything you need to know about the UN’s nature summit Supported by About this content Patrick Greenfield Mon 19 Oct 2026 06.16 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google P assersby could smell the dead fish before they saw them. In August, more than 3,000 pike, roach, carp and rudd were found lifeless along the River Wensum in Norwich. Some gasped for air in their final moments, desperate for the oxygen that heatwave conditions had depleted in the water. Investigators believe that the die-off was triggered by heavy rainfall that flushed through high concentrations of pollution at a time when wildlife were already struggling. The 45-mile (70km) chalk river is one of about 250 in the country. They are a geological accident almost unique to Britain – and one of Earth’s rarest habitats. They emerge from chalk aquifers and are home to species such as freshwater shrimp, otters and stoneflies, also providing drinking water for millions of people. But just 11 have formal protection, with many ravaged by sewage pollution and overextraction. The Norfolk river is one of the few that does have legal protection, but it is in poor ecological health. “We are a world away from the crystal clear, free flowing and mineral-rich waters they could, and should be,” says Eliot Lyne, head of the Norfolk Wildlife Trust. This decade was meant to signal a change in humanity’s relationship with the natural world. At the end of 2022, nearly every government on Earth committed to an ambitious deal to better protect the world’s rapidly disappearing biodiversity at a summit in Montreal, Canada. Negotiators shook hands on targets that included protecting 30% of the planet for nature, restoring nearly a third of the planet’s most degraded ecosystems, and reforming at least $500bn (£375bn) of environmentally harmful subsidies. Some scientists say that we are living through the largest loss of life since the time of the dinosaurs, putting a million species at risk of extinction. This time, humanity is the meteor. The Montreal agreement was the response. View image in fullscreen The leadership of the COP15 biodiversity conference celebrates passing the deal setting this decade’s global targets in Montreal, Canada, December 2022. Photograph: IISD But four years later, governments look almost certain to miss nearly all of the deal’s targets – potentially continuing the record of never having met a single UN target on nature since the biodiversity convention was created at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992. The UK, one of the loudest voices demanding ambition in Montreal, is on track to meet just three of the 23 targets by the end of the decade. This week, countries gather at Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, to decide what to do next. On the eve of the summit, at the launch of a report showing just how far off track the world is on meeting those commitments, António Guterres, secretary general of the UN, warned that lack of progress means “the war on nature has not ended” and that “nature will not survive on good intentions”. Following this, in an address to leaders at an event in Armenia , Guterres once again emphasised the importance of action on subsidies in particular. “Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide,” Guterres said. “They are boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity.
